name: Purikura

card.summary: Japanese sticker-photo booths whose built-in retouching brightens eyes, softens blemishes and lets users decorate the result, so the printed photo shows a polished version of the face.
card.aka: Sticker photo booth, Print Club, print club photos
card.note: Retouching changes the photo, not the face.

quick.overview:
Purikura are Japanese photo booths that print small sticker photos with beautifying effects. Sega and Atlus launched the first, Print Club, in February 1995, and the machines became extremely popular with young people in Japan.

The booths help people look better in photos: they can brighten the image, make eyes sparkle, add colour to lips, blur blemishes and replace backgrounds, then let users decorate the picture with stamps and pens. Similar retouching later became standard in selfie apps.
quick.how: Users pose in a booth, choose their best shots on a touchscreen, then decorate them with stamps, borders and pens before printing sticker sheets, with some machines sending images to phones. Costumes, wigs and multiple camera angles are offered on newer machines.
quick.risks: Nothing physical is involved; the effect exists only in the photo, so the image can differ from how the person looks in person.

lead: Purikura (short for 'print club') are photo booths that produce decorated sticker photos. The first machine, Print Club, was released by Sega and Atlus in February 1995 after Atlus employee Sasaki Miho proposed the idea in 1994 [1]. It became the top-grossing arcade title in Japan in 1996, and Sega earned an estimated 25 billion yen from purikura sales in 1997 alone [1].

For looks, the draw is automatic retouching. Some sticker machines brighten pictures, make eyes sparkle more, change hair, add colour to lips and blur blemishes, and users pick their best shots and decorate them on a touchscreen [1]. Wikipedia credits purikura with inspiring selfie-style features later used by apps such as Instagram and Snapchat [1].

chain: Automatic filters brighten, smooth and decorate the image
Printed photo shows a polished look
angle.text: The booth's retouching and decoration make the printed picture look brighter and smoother than a plain snapshot, changing how the person appears in the photo.

paras: Modern machines let users choose shots, add stamps, clip art, borders and pens on a touchscreen, and can replace backgrounds or offer costumes and wigs [1].

Photo booths date to 1925, when Anatol Josepho opened the first modern booth on Broadway [1]. The Japanese purikura boom began in 1995, and the format spread across Asia; Korean-style 'four-cut' booths grew rapidly in the late 2010s and reached Hong Kong, Singapore, the US and the UK [1]. Wikipedia describes graffiti purikura as a way for young women to challenge traditional gender expectations [1].
